reasoning_summary:
Step-by-step verification of the double-counting argument for n=1012, ground set [2n]=[2024].

0005-0009 (construction): with n even, |A|=|B|=|C|=|D|=506 partitioning [2024], each of A∪C, A∪D, B∪C, B∪D has size 1012, and any three of them intersect in the empty set (e.g. (A∪C)∩(A∪D)=A, and A∩(B∪C)=∅). So 4 is achievable. Justified.

0015-0021 (setup/count): incidence matrix with k rows (subsets) and 2n columns (elements); column sum c_i = number of chosen subsets containing element i, so Σc_i = kn; column i contributes C(c_i,3) all-ones row-triples. Justified.

0023 (Jensen): Σ C(c_i,3) ≥ 2n·C((k/2),3) using the convex extension g(x)=0 for x≤2, x(x-1)(x-2)/6 for x>2, which agrees with C(c,3) at nonnegative integers (note 0070 addresses exactly this technicality). For the case of interest k≥5 we have k/2>2 so g(k/2)=C(k/2,3). Justified.

0027 (upper bound): three subsets meet in ≤1 element, so each row-triple is realized in ≤1 column, giving ≤ C(k,3) triples. Justified.

0029 (algebra): 2n·C(k/2,3) = n·k(k-2)(k-4)/24 ≤ k(k-1)(k-2)/6; dividing by k(k-2)/6 > 0 gives n(k-4)/4 ≤ k-1, i.e. 2n ≤ 8(k-1)/(k-4) for k>4. I recomputed this and it is exactly right.

0031-0035 (conclusion): the stated line contains two transcription slips — for k=5 the RHS is 8·4/1 = 32, not 8·5 = 40, and the comparison symbol is written backwards (it should read RHS < 2·1012 = 2024). Neither affects validity: 8(k-1)/(k-4) = 8 + 24/(k-4) is decreasing in k, so for every k ≥ 5 the RHS is at most 32 (at most 40 even by the author's own value), far below 2n = 2024, contradicting 0029. Hence k ≤ 4, matching the construction, so the answer 4 is correct. The author's threshold 'n ≥ 21' in 0035 is consistent with their value 40 (n ≤ 20) and is a true, merely non-tight, claim (the sharp threshold from the correct value 32 is n ≥ 17); n = 1012 is comfortably covered either way. I sanity-checked the bound independently: 5 subsets would force Σc_i = 5060, while at most C(5,3)=10 elements can have c_i ≥ 3, giving Σc_i ≤ 2·2014 + 5·10 = 4078 < 5060.

BONUS section (0039-0067, about n=3, not needed for the posed problem): the pair-counting bound k·C(n,2) ≤ 2·C(2n,2), i.e. k ≤ 4(2n-1)/(n-1), and its value 10 at n=3 are correct, as is the 10-set example in 0059 and the pigeonhole argument in 0065-0066. One misstatement: 0055 says every element appears in exactly 3 subsets at equality; with k=10, n=3 the incidence count is 30 over 6 elements, i.e. 5 subsets per element (and the author's own list in 0059 has each element in 5 sets). This is a false side remark in auxiliary material and is not used anywhere in the proof of the actual claim.

Overall: the main argument (construction + double count) is sound and gives the correct answer 4; the defects found are transcription-level slips (a flipped inequality symbol / 8·5 for 8·4 in 0031, and 3 for 5 in the bonus equality condition 0055) that do not break any load-bearing deduction.
